title: Cognitive Bifurcation: Dual-Progressive Causal Diffusion with Hippocampal Memory for Continual Graph Learning

problem.claim: Continual Graph Learning on non-stationary streams must adapt to complex distribution shifts while avoiding catastrophic forgetting caused by entangled invariant causal structures and transient environmental noise.

gap.claim: Existing methods based on incremental updates or raw replay are vulnerable to recursive error accumulation, in which early shift misinterpretations propagate and degrade structural understanding.

contributions.claim: The paper proposes DCDHippo, a dual-progressive causal diffusion framework with hippocampal memory for continual graph learning.

The framework combines Progressive Causal Masking for dynamically pruning shift-induced noise and extracting invariant causal skeletons with Causal-Anisotropic Diffusion for reconstructing a global invariant representation space.
The Evolving Hippocampal Memory re-activates global knowledge and distills it back into the fast adapter for adaptation to continuous distribution shifts.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that extensive experiments show DCDHippo significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in adaptability and knowledge retention.

narrative_sequence.summary: Continual graph learning under non-stationary streams faces distribution shifts and catastrophic forgetting.
Incremental updates and raw replay can accumulate errors recursively and cause structural collapse.
The paper proposes DCDHippo as a cognitive-bifurcation-inspired framework.
Fast masking extracts causal skeletons, slow diffusion internalizes them globally, and hippocampal memory feeds global knowledge back to the adapter.
The authors report improved adaptability and knowledge retention relative to state-of-the-art methods.

source_observation.claim: The framework separates rapid shift handling from slower global knowledge consolidation and uses memory to connect the two systems.

interpretation.claim: Separating local adaptation from global consolidation may reduce the propagation of early shift errors while preserving stable structure.

application.claim: Continual learning systems could consider distinct fast and slow processes with an explicit mechanism for transferring consolidated knowledge back to the adaptive component.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this separation improves performance across different shift types or domains.

unknowns: Datasets, distribution-shift settings, baselines, metrics, and numerical results are not specified.
The abstract does not provide implementation details, ablations, or evidence isolating the contributions of the individual modules.
The nature of the reported adaptability and knowledge-retention improvements is not independently verified.
